articles.title: Cities on screen: 10 takes on Chicago
articles.content: Cities on screen: 10 takes on Chicago on x (opens in a new window) Cities on screen: 10 takes on Chicago on facebook (opens in a new window) Cities on screen: 10 takes on Chicago on linkedin (opens in a new window) Cities on screen: 10 takes on Chicago on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Cities on screen: 10 takes on Chicago on x (opens in a new window) Cities on screen: 10 takes on Chicago on facebook (opens in a new window) Cities on screen: 10 takes on Chicago on linkedin (opens in a new window) Cities on screen: 10 takes on Chicago on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Danny Leigh Published September 3 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Stay informed with free updates Simply sign up to the Film myFT Digest -- delivered directly to your inbox. This article is part of FT Globetrotter’s guide to Chicago I know Chicago better through movies than bricks and mortar. My loss, I know. (Truly, on every visit I’ve always wanted to stay longer.) But so many films set in the city are so stellar that it’s almost too easy to visit Chicago cinematically instead. Of course, the film version is rife with organised crime. But the singular nature of Chicago on screen involves so much else besides: architecture, jazz, sport, comedy, and the spirit of grind that earned it the nickname “The City That Works”. I write this knowing not everyone will forgive my omissions. So many great Chicago films are people’s personal favourites and they can’t all be included. I could, for instance, fill this list entirely with the work of Chicago’s film-maker laureate, the late John Hughes. But it feels unreasonable to have more than one film per director, even if that means losing Sixteen Candles , Pretty in Pink , Home Alone and The Breakfast Club. (Ouch.) While I’m making excuses, including The Dark Knight felt like selling the city short, given that it merely stands in for Gotham. But there are other beloved Chicago movies not listed here — The Sting , The Fugitive , the eponymous Chicago — about which I can only say that this is the problem with too much of a good thing. I hope the films that are here make up for it. It’s a collection of movies set in my kind of town, a Chicago I’ve got to know in darkened rooms. ‘Ferris Bueller’s Day Off’ (John Hughes, 1986) Matthew Broderick, Mia Sara and Alan Ruck swap school for the Art Institute of Chicago in ‘Ferris Bueller’s Day Off’ © Allstar Picture Library/Alamy Matthew Broderick’s teen renegade Ferris Bueller will always be a great advert for truancy, and the movie that bears his name is also the most impassioned ode to Chicago in this entire list. It is also surely the pinnacle of director John Hughes’s career of love letters to the city. The ride that starts in a borrowed Ferrari down the Edens Expressway takes in the Sears Tower Observatory, Chicago Stock Exchange, Art Institute of Chicago and a trip to Wrigley Field to watch the Cubs. I was 14 when the movie came out — part of a generation who would forever associate the city with the timeless glory of skipping school. Where to watch: Paramount+ ‘Scarface’ (Howard Hawks, 1932) A poster for the original 1932 ‘Scarface’ movie, with Paul Muni as the Al Capone figure Tony Camonte © Chronicle/Alamy In April 1932, the original Scarface arrived hot off the presses. Its anti-hero Tony Camonte was never officially acknowledged as modelled after Al Capone, but the resemblance caused a sensation, given that the film arrived just as Capone was finally heading to jail. (An old rumour had it that Capone eventually saw and enjoyed the movie enough to source his own private copy, though sadly, that probably owes more to myth than reality.) Not one scene was shot in the actual city, as was standard practice in early Hollywood. But spiritually, Chicago brooded from every frame. Where to watch: Amazon Prime Video ‘Hoop Dreams’ (Steve James, 1994) Arthur Agee in basketball documentary ‘Hoop Dreams’ © Sipa US/Alamy Chicago is really multiple Chicagos — a point made unforgettably in Hoop Dreams , one of the greatest documentaries ever made in any city. The subjects are William Gates and Arthur Agee, two Black teenagers from the hard-edged worlds of Cabrini-Green and West Garfield Park with a rare gift on the basketball court. Each aspiring to make it in the NBA, both are recruited to play for a prestigious school team in prosperous suburban Westchester. From here, the human drama would have been impossible to script. More fool Hollywood that somehow the movie wasn’t even nominated for a Best Documentary Oscar. Where to watch: Apple TV ‘Thief’ (Michael Mann, 1981) James Caan and James Belushi in Michael Mann’s ‘Thief’ © Everett Collection/Alamy Think of director Michael Mann and you think of LA. You can blame that on Heat and Collateral , movies that made this bravura talent synonymous with Tinseltown. But consider yourself misdirected. For one thing, Mann himself is a product of Humboldt Park. (Locals report you can still hear his upbringing in his pronunciation of “Chi-caw-go.”) For another, the movie that announced him as a film-maker, Thief , is also a defining portrait of Chicago. James Caan plays a safe-cracker making one last score, inspired by figures from the actual local underworld — some of whom were “technical advisers” on the film. The mastery of night and light that Mann would bring to LA was clearly first trained on the smokestacks and sidewalks of his home city. Where to watch: Tubi , Apple TV ‘Candyman’ (Nia DaCosta, 2021) Nia DaCosta’s remake of the horror classic ‘Candyman’ plays out among a community of artists in the now-gentrified Chicago neighbourhood of Cabrini-Green © Album/Alamy Make no mistake, the original 1992 Candyman is a fine horror movie, a deft piece of mythmaking grounded in the complex realities of Chicago. Say “Candyman” five times in the mirror, a local fable says, and a gruesome end will find you — a nightmare bound up with America’s past, here in the stark housing projects of Cabrini-Green. But I’m actually including Nia DaCosta’s jagged 2021 remake, which brings both the story and the portrait of the city up to date. The urban legend of Cabrini-Green returns — but gentrification has taken root between films. A city as old and grand as Chicago can transform, the movie says. History, though, lives on. Where to watch: YouTube , Apple TV ‘The Blues Brothers’ (John Landis, 1980) Aretha Franklin in the famous Nate’s diner scene in ‘The Blue Brothers’ © AJ Pics/Alamy Did any film ever play such a mad ambassadorial role for a city as The Blues Brothers ? The characters of Jake and Elwood Blues, played by John Belushi (whose family was from Humboldt Park) and Dan Aykroyd, started out on Saturday Night Live , airing from New York, but their instant cult favourite of a movie has proved to be an eternal showcase for Chicago. Sometimes, the homage was subtle. Only a local would have recognised Nate’s Deli on Maxwell Street in the scene where Aretha Franklin demands of her husband: “Think” (“about what you’re trying to do to me”). At other points, there was no doubt. The Daley Plaza finale involved 200 National Guardsmen, one hundred cops and a SWAT team in Sherman tanks, helicopters, fire trucks and squad cars. Where to watch: Amazon Prime Video , Apple TV ‘Love Jones’ (Theodore Witcher, 1997) Larenz Tate and Nia Long in the rain-soaked but ‘daisy-fresh’ indie romance ‘Love Jones’ © Cinematic/Alamy Movie types get misty-eyed about 1990s US indie cinema, making it all the stranger that Love Jones still flies under the radar. Then again, the film was always a one-off — a daisy-fresh romantic comedy, built around Black characters who swerved the gangsta clichés that were then thriving at the box office. Instead, the film had the flawless chemistry of stars Nia Long and Larenz Tate, and a wry Chicago realism. On location across the city, the weather was so hostile that the rain had to be written into the script; Long played the final scene with a warming layer of garbag

articles.title: Business school teaching case study: Can you put a price on impact?
articles.content: Products derived from ucuuba trees play a crucial role in Amazonian communities © Shutterstock Business school teaching case study: Can you put a price on impact? on x (opens in a new window) Business school teaching case study: Can you put a price on impact? on facebook (opens in a new window) Business school teaching case study: Can you put a price on impact? on linkedin (opens in a new window) Business school teaching case study: Can you put a price on impact? on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Business school teaching case study: Can you put a price on impact? on x (opens in a new window) Business school teaching case study: Can you put a price on impact? on facebook (opens in a new window) Business school teaching case study: Can you put a price on impact? on linkedin (opens in a new window) Business school teaching case study: Can you put a price on impact? on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Christopher Marquis , Cambridge Judge Business School Published September 3 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. The concept of the “bioeconomy” — building wealth from a living forest rather than a cleared one — reached a milestone last year with its discussion at the COP30 summit in Brazil. Few businesses have staked more on the idea than Natura, the Brazilian cosmetics group. The company has spent 26 years sourcing ingredients from Amazon communities and, for a decade, trying to show in hard numbers that a standing tree is worth more than a felled one. Its instrument is called Integrated Profit & Loss, or IP&L: a methodology that puts a monetary value on the social, human and environmental effects of everything it does — from the incomes of millions of direct-sales consultants, through its factories, to the carbon in its supply chain and the forest its contracts keep protecting. When Natura published its first IP&L in 2021, it reckoned that every Brazilian real (R$) of sales generated about R$1.5 ($0.29) of value for society, and by 2025 the figure had reached R$4 — a target originally set for 2030, met five years early. The IP&L is among the most developed experiments in impact accounting anywhere. It is also a test of a larger claim: that if a business states what it does to the world in the same units as profit, sustainability can finally be part of the decisions that matter — for example, which ingredients to buy and how to pay employees. Test yourself This is part of a series of regular business school-style teaching case studies devoted to business dilemmas. Read the text and the articles from the FT and elsewhere suggested at the end (and linked to within the piece) before considering the questions raised. The series forms part of a wide-ranging collection of FT “instant teaching case studies” that explore business challenges. Founded in 1969 and selling door-to-door since 1974, Natura built a business on ingredients such as ucuuba, andiroba and açaí, gathered by more than 10,000 families across the Amazon. Its logic prioritises the standing forest: a tree cut for timber earns a farmer a few dollars once, while the same tree harvested for its seeds can pay several times as much, year after year. That model helped make Natura, in 2014, the first publicly traded company to certify as a B Corp , and later the largest; it recertified most recently in 2024. The IP&L grew out of that history. Working with the Capitals Coalition and the specialist firm Valuing Impact , Natura began with an environmental account in the mid-2010s, added social and human dimensions, and built an economic valuation model covering its whole value chain — sourcing, operations, consultants, product use and disposal. A young açaí picker works on the land in the municipality of Manacapuru in the Brazilian state of Amazonas © Alessandro Falco/FT Impacts were translated into financial terms through valuation factors: a social cost of carbon, a per-hectare value for conserved forest, health-adjusted measures of income and wellbeing. In one example , the model estimates that consuming 300,000kg of diesel produces 1.38mn kg of carbon dioxide equivalent; applying a factor of R$2.97 per kilogramme values the climate damage at R$4.1mn. Adding particulate pollution, fossil-resource depletion and 14 other environmental effects brings the estimated loss of societal wellbeing to R$12.46mn. The calculation in effect assigns a societal cost of roughly R$41.5 for every kilogramme of diesel consumed, once climate, pollution, resource depletion and other impacts are included. Natura’s claim is that the IP&L can provide a roadmap to run the business rather than merely reporting on it. Procurement and finance teams use it to weigh options in a common currency. Ana Costa, a sustainability executive at Natura, said the exercise focused the company on the question of “are we creating more value than we extract from the world?” adding that “if you do not measure it, it does not matter”. For example, in 2025, it calculated that its higher-level sales consultants generated an estimated R$42.7bn in positive human capital impact through things such as the value of training and how their living conditions compare with standards benchmarked by region. Conversely, product use and end-of-life disposal depleted natural capital by R$5.1bn due to the water, waste and emissions expended as consumers use and discard its products. The calculation forces the company to ask different questions than it otherwise would: Do higher sales leave its consultants better off? And are the products behind those sales — from the palm oil in them to the packaging thrown away afterwards — doing more damage in water, waste and emissions than the revenue justifies? Sceptics doubt that summary figures decide anything. The headline result is a net number and Natura’s natural capital is still negative , offset by positives in human and social capital. If the number that gets quoted blends the good with the bad, does the IP&L sharpen the company’s priorities or soften them? Would it reduce scrutiny on the biggest negative impacts — scope-three emissions [those that occur indirectly across a company’s broader value chain] from inputs such as palm oil, or the disposal of products after sale? A second tension lies in the valuation factors. Someone must decide what a hectare of rainforest, a year of a consultant’s income or a tonne of carbon is worth, and those judgments and the research underlying them are contestable. The results sit apart from audited financial statements and cannot easily be compared with those of the few other companies attempting this method. Valuing impacts is a growing trend. Other companies such as Philips , Novo Nordisk and Kering have published EP&L (environmental profit-and-loss) accounts, which convert carbon emissions, pollution and resource use into monetary terms. AkzoNobel , the Dutch paints and coatings group, is among the closest precedents, working to publish an IP&L covering environmental, social and human impacts. Natura’s approach is to open up the tool to other users. In July 2026 it launched The Future P&L , a free platform that lets any company enter data on its workforce, suppliers, waste and social spending to see the effects expressed in money. Natura says the approach has revealed more than $9bn of accumulated positive impact and hopes wider use will move investors and regulators towards accounting systems that recognise social, human and environmental impacts While Natura’s impact is real — its Amazon sourcing sustains communities and forest, and its network moves genuine income to millions of women — the open question is narrower and harder. When a company translates that impact into money, does the figure become an instrument that changes what it sources, makes and pays — or a story it tells about itself, that still sits alongside a strategy decided in the o

articles.title: The mysterious billionaire and Cuba’s cigar industry
articles.content: The mysterious billionaire and Cuba’s cigar industry on x (opens in a new window) The mysterious billionaire and Cuba’s cigar industry on facebook (opens in a new window) The mysterious billionaire and Cuba’s cigar industry on linkedin (opens in a new window) The mysterious billionaire and Cuba’s cigar industry on whatsapp (opens in a new window) The mysterious billionaire and Cuba’s cigar industry on x (opens in a new window) The mysterious billionaire and Cuba’s cigar industry on facebook (opens in a new window) The mysterious billionaire and Cuba’s cigar industry on linkedin (opens in a new window) The mysterious billionaire and Cuba’s cigar industry on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Jack Adamović Davies Published September 3 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. From his perch in the corner, fumes wisping up past his frameless glasses, Mitchell Orchant puffs contentedly on an imposing Hoyo De Monterrey Epicure No 3 as he surveys his compact kingdom. Three decades ago he founded the C.Gars chain of tobacconists, and this is his flagship store in the smart St James’s district of central London. Smoke from the stick — 2cm wide, 12cm long — drifts through the air to a filter, passing between two framed pictures. One is a Cuban flag rendered from blue, white and red smoke, the other a monochrome photo from the country’s 1950s revolution. They are unusual adornments for a shop not far from the Ritz hotel and a caviar emporium. “It’s the most incredible symbol of capitalism produced in one of the last bastions of communism,” says Orchant, elegantly folded into his armchair like the silk handkerchief in his breast pocket. “It’s just one of those bizarre things, isn’t it? They make the finest cigars in the world. It’s a product they need to sell because they need the currency.” Havana has been the subject of a US embargo for more than six decades, which has cost the Cuban economy at least $1tn, according to the country’s estimates. For a nation that struggles to keep the lights on, cigars are a vital source of revenue. The ruling Communist party runs the island’s tobacco industry as a monopoly, which for a long time generated a reliable half a billion dollars in revenue each year. In April 2022, that income stream was turbocharged after the company charged with marketing and distributing Cuba’s cigars, Habanos, decreed that prices would go up steeply, including for its most cherished offerings, such as the Cohiba and Trinidad marques. By 2024, the most recent year for which figures are available, Habanos’s annual revenue had reached $827mn. “It was a very clever thing that they did,” Orchant says. “It didn’t make any difference to sales at all, other than that sales increased and perhaps they became more aspirational for certain niches of clients.” Cigar quality is checked at the Cohiba factory in Havana in 2022 © Yamil Lage/AFP via Getty Images Cigars are shaking off their reputation as an old, rich man’s hobby: Orchant’s clients in their twenties tend to buy online, and the demographic coming into his shop, a customer every 20 minutes that afternoon, skews middle-aged. He insists the cigar lounge is inherently democratic. “Whatever your background is, it doesn’t make any difference. You’re rich, you’re poor, you’re this religion, that religion. Leftwing, rightwing, everyone has a nice conversation,” says Orchant. “I think it’s a good leveller, a cigar.” But behind the egalitarianism of a cigar is the story of an opaque investment by a mysterious tycoon — one who has recently experienced a most precipitous fall. In 1492, Christopher Columbus was awestruck when he came upon Cuba’s lush tropical shores. He had “never beheld such a beautiful place”, the ship’s journal recorded him saying. The following week, his crew members encountered “men and women with a half-burnt weed in their hands”. The weed was, of course, tobacco. It had first arrived on Cuba from the Andes four thousand years earlier, and archaeological remains suggest it has played a role in the island’s culture since at least the ninth century. It did not take long for the Europeans to develop a taste for cigars, whose name derives from the Mayan verb describing the act of smoking rolled tobacco leaves. Spanish colonists began growing tobacco in Cuba during the 16th century, with commercial production established by its final decades. The subsequent centuries of selective breeding and experimentation laid the foundations for modern cigars, according to Charlie Minato, co-founder and editor of the US-based Halfwheel cigar news website. “This seed that we use for cigar tobacco is not the same as what you would use for cigarette tobacco, nor is it the same as what you would use for pipe tobacco,” he says. “The seed that we’re using for cigar tobacco — or at least its ‘Genesis mother seed’ — was developed in Cuba.” The result is a distinctive flavour. “I can, for the most part, tell within 90 seconds whether or not a cigar is Cuban. A lot of times I can do it before even lighting up. There is something different about that tobacco; it has a sweetness to it.” So unique is the Cuban experience that in February 1962 US President John F Kennedy summoned his press secretary, Pierre Salinger, for a special mission. “I need a lot of cigars,” Salinger recalled Kennedy saying. Specifically, the president wanted 1,000 Cuban-made Petit Upmanns by the following morning. Returning successful the next day, the press secretary finally understood the significance of his assignment. “Kennedy smiled, and opened up his desk,” Salinger wrote. “He took out a long paper which he immediately signed. It was the decree banning all Cuban products from the United States. Cuban cigars were now illegal in our country.” President John F Kennedy © Bettmann Archive/Getty Images The embargo remains in place today. Nonetheless, demand is strong in America. “Up until very recently it was quite clear that the US was ultimately the largest market for Cuban cigars even though it’s illegal,” says Minato. “There are tens of thousands of people who are going to smoke a Cuban cigar in the US this week, at a minimum.” Outside America, smokers’ ability to procure Cuban cigars is instead constrained by Cuba’s ability to make them. A large part of the problem is that much of the infrastructure for producing what an economist has disparagingly termed “Cuba’s centrally planned cigar” is stuck deep in the 20th century. While tobacco growers across Latin America employ John Deere tractors, Cuba’s work with mules and carts, says Laurence Davis, owner of the Sautter Cigars shop in London. “There’s been no investment; they’re still seeding by hand.” Today, while Cuban cigars are regarded as the blueprint from which all others have evolved, Habanos’s annual revenue is a fraction of the global market, estimated to be worth up to $60bn a year. The world’s top exporter of cigars is the Dominican Republic, which ships roughly 8.4bn sticks a year, dwarfing Habanos’s 70mn. This was the scene — production-constrained, price-constrained — that Chen Zhi entered. © Nicolás Ortega In September 2022, Havana welcomed Cambodian Prime Minister Hun Sen on the second visit of his 38-year premiership. Among the usual entourage of sycophants and bureaucrats aboard the 40-metre Boeing Business Jet was an unusual man. The first thing that set Chen Zhi apart from his fellow passengers was that he was not a native Cambodian. He did have a Cambodian passport — two, in fact, one identifying him as a diplomat — yet he was born in China in 1987 to parents living in a fishing village across the water from Taiwan. Before his 24th birthday, Chen had moved to Cambodia on the advice of a relative interested in purchasing real estate there, according to his lawyers. Whatever led Chen to Cambodia, by 2020 he was doing very well for himself. Neither t

articles.title: Box (BOX) Q2 2027 Earnings Call Transcript
articles.content: Box (BOX) Q2 2027 Earnings Call Transcript Motley Fool Transcribing, The Motley Fool Tue, September 1, 2026 at 6:13 PM EDT 45 min read BOX Image source: The Motley Fool. DATE Tuesday, Aug. 25, 2026 at 5:00 p.m. ET CALL PARTICIPANTS Vice President, Investor Relations - Cynthia Hiponia Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer - Aaron Levie Co-Founder and Chief Financial Officer - Dylan Smith Full Conference Call Transcript Cynthia Hiponia: Good afternoon, and welcome to Box's Second Quarter Fiscal 2027 Earnings Conference Call. I'm Cynthia Hiponia, Vice President, Investor Relations. On the call today, we have Aaron Levie, Box Co-Founder and CEO; and Dylan Smith, Box Co-Founder and CFO. Following our prepared remarks, we will take your questions. Today's call is being webcast and will also be available for replay on our IR website. Supplemental slides are now available on our website. On this call, we will be making forward-looking statements, including our third quarter and full fiscal year 2027 financial guidance and our expectations regarding our financial performance for fiscal 2027 in future periods, including gross margins, operating margin, operating leverage, future profitability, net retention rates, remaining performance obligations, revenue and billings and the impact of foreign currency exchange rates and our expectations regarding the size of our market opportunity, including the growing opportunity driven by the increasing role of unstructured data in AI agents in the enterprise, our planned investments, future product offerings, go-to-market initiatives and growth strategies, the timing and market adoption of and benefits from our new products, solutions and pricing models, our ability to address enterprise challenges, including enabling organizations to automate critical workflows and deliver value for our customers. The benefits from our deepening partnerships with leading AI labs, hyperscalers and systems integrators and our capital allocation strategies, including potential repurchase of our common stock and future share count reductions. These statements reflect our best judgment based on factors currently known to us, and actual events or results may differ materially. Please refer to our earnings press release filed today and the risk factors and documents that we file with the SEC including our most recent quarterly report on Form 10-Q for information on risks and uncertainties that may cause actual results to differ materially from statements made on this earnings call. These forward-looking statements are being made as of today, August 25, 2026, and we disclaim any obligation to update or revise them should they change or cease to be up to date. In addition, during today's call, we will discuss non-GAAP financial measures. These non-GAAP financial measures should be considered in addition to and not as a substitute for or in isolation from our GAAP results. You will find additional disclosures regarding these non-GAAP measures, including reconciliations with comparable GAAP results in our earnings press release and in the supplemental slides, which can be found on the Investor Relations page of our website. Unless otherwise indicated, all references to financial measures are on a non-GAAP basis. Story Continues Finally, please see our earnings deck posted on our IR website for a more detailed look at our Q3 and full year '27 guidance. Thank you. With that, let me turn the call over to Aaron. Aaron Levie: Thanks, Cynthia, and thank you all for joining the call today. Box delivered exceptional second quarter results, continuing the strong momentum we saw in Q1 and led by the rapid customer adoption of Enterprise Advanced. Second quarter revenue exceeded our guidance, growing 9% year-over-year or 11% in constant currency and produced operating margins of 29%. We drove a net retention rate of 106% ahead of our expectations of 105%, driven by both price per seat increases and seat expansion. Our Q2 billings growth of 17% year-over-year and RPO growth of 15% year-over-year reflect the success of our strategic investments in both go-to-market and product road map in delivering solutions to customers that address their most critical challenges in AI. Some examples of our Enterprise Advanced wins in the quarter included a leading multinational investment bank that upgraded from Enterprise Plus to Enterprise Advanced transitioning its legacy file servers to Box Platform. This deployment will expand its license to a wall-to-wall agreement to deliver unstructured data insights across its global banking teams. Next, a major federal agency upgraded from Enterprise Plus to Enterprise Advanced with a 4x seat expansion to replace its legacy contract life cycle management and collaboration platforms. In partnership with Salesforce, Box will power secure Claude-based CLM and document management across key legal and research divisions, replacing multiple SaaS vendors. This agency-wide modernization is enabled by Box's FedRAMP High compliance, our secure identity verified e-signatures and Enterprise Advanced capabilities. With record Q2 bookings these wins and many others make it clear that our role in enabling enterprises to get the most out of their enterprise content and transform in the era of AI is becoming increasingly significant. During the second quarter, I spoke with many enterprise technology leaders who highlighted their primary goals and challenges in implementing AI. One of the most common topics is how enterprises can get the right context to AI agents in a secure and governed way as well as tap into the full value of their unstructured data. To do this, enterprises need a secure platform that can connect all the intelligence and capabilities of AI models to enterprise content and workflows. The world's most advanced super intelligence is only as useful as the underlying enterprise knowledge and corporate information that it has access to. Instead of companies sitting on millions or hundreds of millions of files that they know very little about with AI agents, they can now ask questions about this data, mine it all for intelligence and automate nearly any workflow that involves this enterprise content. This is the intelligent content management platform that we are building. These technology leaders that I'm speaking with are also recognizing that as AI model capabilities advance rapidly across an expanding set of vendors like OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, xAI, NVIDIA and more, that enterprises will need a model neutral platform that connects their content and workflows through these models and agents securely. With AI costs continuing to rise, the ability to draw the right cost performance mix with any vendor becomes essential rather than migrating content and workflows into separate systems to unlock AI's benefits, our intelligent content management platform gives enterprises a single platform where they can swap models or agents on their content at any time securely. Now Box is at the center of the greatest transformation in how enterprises work, and we are continuing to drive our product and go-to-market strategies to take full advantage of this massive opportunity. Building on our product leadership. In the second quarter, we announced a range of new capabilities that help customers transform the value of their content with AI. We introduced new security capabilities designed to give organizations greater control over AI agents working with their enterprise content with new agent guardrails, third-party agent activity oversight, prompt injection detection agent classification-based access policies and more customers will be able to extend Box's enterprise-grade security controls to both Box Agents and third-party agents such as Claude, ChatGPT, Gemini and more. articles.title: Where does Charlotte Rampling get her jackets? Autista
articles.content: Where does Charlotte Rampling get her jackets? Autista on x (opens in a new window) Where does Charlotte Rampling get her jackets? Autista on facebook (opens in a new window) Where does Charlotte Rampling get her jackets? Autista on linkedin (opens in a new window) Where does Charlotte Rampling get her jackets? Autista on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Where does Charlotte Rampling get her jackets? Autista on x (opens in a new window) Where does Charlotte Rampling get her jackets? Autista on facebook (opens in a new window) Where does Charlotte Rampling get her jackets? Autista on linkedin (opens in a new window) Where does Charlotte Rampling get her jackets? Autista on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Inès Cross Published September 3 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page Unlock the Editor’s Digest for free Roula Khalaf, Editor of the FT, selects her favourite stories in this weekly newsletter. Dune Chambaud always knew she was going to start her own brand but it took the perfect location to spark the right idea. Two years ago, while walking in her neighbourhood, the antiquarian district of Paris’s Saint-Germain-des-Prés, she discovered an old clock store on a quiet street corner was for sale. “I just had this feeling I had to do something with it, before anyone else did,” she says. With three days to make a proposition to the owner, she asked herself: “What do people desire? What do I desire? What do I value?” Out of this came the phrase: rare things for rare people. “I imagined it was probably going to be something with clothing and objects, or maybe something jewel-like,” she says. The fluorescent “cabinet of curiosities” at Autista © Celia Spenard-Ko Today the four-storey sandstone building is home to her clothing brand Autista , which for the past two years has sold just one item: Alpine-style Janker hunting jackets, inspired by one worn by Chambaud’s father, and also by the late Hubert de Givenchy, whose wardrobe she had long admired. “I always had this desire to create long-lasting, great-quality garments,” says Chambaud. “I tried to get the experience in everything that it would take to one day build a brand.” Over the years, she had collected different versions of the jackets, some with beautiful box-pleats, piping, an inclined lapel or more military-style stand-up collars. They inspired the style she has created for today. “Just to be clear, I am a pacifist,” she says. “But I am drawn to the craftsmanship involved.” The shopfront on rue de Beaune Autista founder Dune Chambaud wears The Verneuil Club 12 jacket, €4,850 © Celia Spenard-Ko Chambaud designed the storefront to be as inconspicuous as possible. The glass is tinted, there’s no product in the windows, and the brand’s logo is embossed on the façade in the same stone. “The people who come inside tend to be very bold,” she says. As luck would have it, her first customer happened to be her muse: Charlotte Rampling . “When I tell this story, it doesn’t sound true.” Those who do enter will be surprised by the interiors, which have a sleek, futuristic bent. The front showroom space features a resin floor littered with silver petals; on the walls hang three “cabinets of curiosities” each containing the brand’s signature Club jacket, framed by ultraviolet light. At night, the store glimmers. Merino wool The Verneuil Club 12 jackets, €4,850 each © Benedikt Ahmed Frank In the centre of the showroom, a chrome vitrine houses rows of handmade buttons shaped in a quadruple of the letter “A” from the brand’s gothic logo. Original fastenings on Janker jackets tend to be big and bulky, often made from horn or cast metal; Autista’s are moulded in pearl, precious metals and imitation Bohemian uranium glass. They are hand-sewn onto the jackets with a special waxed-cotton and linen thread. The Club jackets come with the option of 10, 12, or 17 buttons and contrasting collars. Prices start from €3,850; the more decadent styles can cost upwards of €15,000. Fabrics include an extra-fine merino wool (wearable for most of the year) and exclusive Japanese blends such as a linen and rami mix, which looks similar to denim. Each style has six functional pockets. “People always talk about how they want women to be free but then they sell us handbags,” says Chambaud. “I want jackets with pockets!” A fluorescent Krypton button on the back of an Osaka Club 12 jacket, €3,850 © Benedikt Ahmed Frank Merino wool women’s The Autista Club 17 jacket, €9,500 © Benedikt Ahmed Frank Autista also offers custom orders and a made-to-measure service at its downstairs atelier. A mezzanine, painted a rich velvety brown inspired by the colour of a 1970s Porsche, is for VIP appointments and fittings. After two years of perfecting her hero product, Chambaud is now expanding the range with a line of shirting and pyjamas (from €1,250), in a cotton poplin and linen melange, and more jewellery-style buttons. And Rampling, for whom Autista has created bespoke pieces including a linen shirt with a double-stand collar and a jacket with a new chain-link button, is fronting the autumn campaign. “When Charlotte first walked into the store, she also picked up the jacket that I had designed for her in my mind,” says Chambaud. “She is always the first to try something new.” Reuse this content (opens in new window) Comments Jump to comments section Follow the topics in this article Style Fashion Paris HTSI Inès Cross Comments

articles.title: Can Better Star Ratings and Margin Expansion Drive Humana (HUM) Higher?
articles.content: Can Better Star Ratings and Margin Expansion Drive Humana (HUM) Higher? Soumya Eswaran Thu, September 3, 2026 at 10:34 AM EDT 3 min read HUM Eagle Capital Management , an investment management company, released its second quarter 2026 investor letter. A copy of the letter can be downloaded here . In the quarter, Eagle Capital Management discussed how enthusiasm around AI capital spending has driven strong S&P 500 earnings growth while also increasing risks from elevated valuations, concentrated demand, and aggressive investment assumptions. Eagle remains a strong believer in AI but prefers constructing a portfolio that can perform across multiple outcomes rather than relying on one forecast. The firm believes current earnings can overstate underlying economics because semiconductor equipment is depreciated over several years, while free cash flow growth remains much weaker. It also expects competition and additional capacity across AI labs, hyperscalers, and semiconductors to eventually create winners and losers. These dynamics are encouraging Eagle to recycle capital toward attractive opportunities outside the most crowded AI trades while maintaining selective exposure to high-quality beneficiaries. The portfolio trades at a 20% market discount with faster expected EPS growth. Please review the Strategy's top five holdings for key selections in 2026. In its second-quarter 2026 investor letter, Eagle Capital Management highlighted Humana Inc. (NYSE: HUM ). Humana Inc. (NYSE:HUM) is an American insurance company that provides medical and specialty insurance products. On September 02, 2026, Humana Inc. (NYSE:HUM) closed at $400.97 per share. Over the past month, Humana Inc. (NYSE:HUM) returned 9.18%, and its shares gained 28.52% over the past 52 weeks. Humana Inc. (NYSE:HUM) has a market capitalization of $48.15 billion with a 52-week trading range between $163.11 and $428.88. Eagle Capital Management stated the following regarding Humana Inc. (NYSE:HUM) in its Q2 2026 investor letter: "Managed care (13% of capital): UnitedHealth Group, Humana Inc. (NYSE:HUM), Elevance: These managed care companies have significant scale advantages in a consolidated industry that outgrows the overall economy. The industry moves with its own cycle and, over the last several years, has faced cost/price pressures in Medicare Advantage and Medicaid. Even the largest firms are earning poor margins, and some weaker firms are unprofitable. We believe conditions have bottomed out and that we are transitioning to a multi-year improvement in margins and earnings. Al-driven technology projects can both reduce costs and improve service quality. Humana is also making good strides, and we expect significantly improved Star ratings for the company later this year. We expect EPS growth of 15-20% over the next several years, driven by moderate revenue growth and significantly expanding margins." Story Continues JPMorgan and Mizuho Raise Humana (HUM) Price Targets as Managed Care Outlook Improves Humana Inc. (NYSE:HUM) is not on our list of the 40 Most Popular Stocks Among Hedge Funds . articles.title: Diversified strikes $1.8bn deal for Permian operator Birch
articles.content: Diversified strikes $1.8bn deal for Permian operator Birch Salong Debbarma Thu, September 3, 2026 at 10:31 AM EDT 3 min read Diversified Energy has agreed to acquire Birch Permian and some affiliated companies (collectively "Birch") from Elliott Investment Management for around $1.8bn. Birch's assets are based in the Permian Basin and are expected to add a significant operated position of proved developed producing (PDP) oil and gas assets to Diversified's US onshore portfolio. The transaction is expected to close during the fourth quarter of 2026, subject to customary closing conditions and regulatory approvals. Diversified intends to fund the acquisition primarily through a privately rated asset-backed securitisation of around $1.5bn, in partnership with Carlyle's Asset-Backed Finance and Capital Markets teams. Additional funding will come from available liquidity under its revolving credit facility and other standard financing sources. The deal includes a $50m break fee. With this acquisition, Diversified expects its pro forma operated gross volumes to reach around 2.5 billion cubic feet equivalent per day (bcfe/d), of which around 1.6bcfe/d is net production. Birch currently produces roughly 68,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day (boepd), with a mix consisting of 38% oil, 32% natural gas liquids (NGLs) and 30% natural gas. The portfolio includes around 480 net wells, mainly mature and low-decline, with proved reserves of approximately 1.17 trillion cubic feet equivalent and estimated annualised adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) of $548m. Integrated infrastructure includes 46,000 net mineral acres of core Permian Basin leasehold, 12 central production facilities, nine gathering facilities and more than 60 miles of gathering pipeline, as well as water disposal and recycling assets. The company anticipates the acquisition will lead to an estimated 35% rise in production volume and a 55% increase in adjusted EBITDA. Diversified has also expanded its partnership with Carlyle , allowing both companies to potentially pursue up to $10bn in additional PDP asset acquisitions subject to agreement and approvals. Diversified chairman and CEO Rusty Hutson said: "I am thrilled to announce the acquisition of Birch, a premier Permian Basin operator that represents an important milestone in Diversified's evolution and long-term growth strategy. This $1.8bn acquisition is our largest in the company's 25-year history. "Birch has assembled one of the highest-quality operated asset positions, combining a concentrated footprint in the core of the Permian, substantial production scale, integrated infrastructure and a track record of delivering predictable, high-margin cash flows. Story Continues "These assets align exceptionally well with our disciplined approach to acquiring and optimising long-life energy assets and provide a compelling platform for future value creation for our shareholders." The board of Diversified has determined that the transaction is in the best interests of its shareholders. Birch's assets are expected to align with Diversified's strategy of acquiring and operating mature, established production supported by comprehensive infrastructure. The portfolio offers opportunities for optimisation, including enhanced oil recovery at more than 150 permitted locations. articles.title: Nvidia confirms $13 billion acquisition of open-weight AI platform Hugging Face
articles.content: Nvidia confirms $13 billion acquisition of open-weight AI platform Hugging Face Jake Conley · Breaking Business News Reporter Thu, September 3, 2026 at 10:28 AM EDT 4 min read NVDA Nvidia ( NVDA ) on Thursday confirmed its plans to acquire the open-weight AI platform Hugging Face for roughly $13 billion, sending shares up more than 1% in early trading. The deal will see Nvidia pay $12.93 billion for the platform, per a press release. More than 18 million developers, researchers, and creators use Hugging Face to share more than 3 million models, and more than 200,000 companies use the platform to discover and deploy AI, Nvidia said. More from Yahoo Scout When will the Hugging Face acquisition be completed? How does this acquisition fit Nvidia's AI platform strategy? Why is Nvidia acquiring Hugging Face for $13 billion? What impact will the deal have on Nvidia's financials? The move highlights how Nvidia has thrown its weight behind open-weight AI models. In a statement, Nvidia said Hugging Face would remain "an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem," that the company would continue to support open-weight and open-source AI models, and that Nvidia itself is the largest contributor of open models and data to the Hugging Face platform. In a call following the announcement, Nvidia enterprise computing general manager Justin Boitano said the company "believe[s] in having a healthy ecosystem of closed models and open models leads to a world where you're going to continue to train these models and run these models at scale." The only way for the Hugging Face user base to grow, Boitano said, is to keep giving those developers optionality in terms of the hardware, clouds, and other parts of the stack that they build on, even if "Nvidia will benefit from the training that's done and the inference that's done on our hardware." "Open models strengthen safety and cybersecurity, accelerate innovation and diffusion, and enable sovereignty," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang posted on X about the acquisition. "They allow every developer, startup, university, industry and country to build with, customize and benefit from AI." The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027, pending regulatory approval. For Nvidia, the deal represents a "great strategic move," BD8 CEO and Nvidia investor Barbara Doran told Yahoo Finance on Thursday, arguing that Nvidia is "positioning themselves to be much more of an AI platform rather than just a supplier of chips." "Right now, chip … demand is huge, but they are positioning themselves for the day when that will slow down," Doran said. That day "still looks like it's far in the future. But that will happen at some point." The move also shouldn't worry investors who might approach the expenditure with some eyebrows raised toward the balance sheet, Doran said. Given Nvidia's free cash flow — expected to reach near $200 billion for fiscal year 2027 — "$13 billion … is not a big bite," Doran told Yahoo Finance. Story Continues The Street seems to be net positive on the news, with Nvidia stock gaining close to 2% in the first hour of Thursday's trading session. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang listens to a question from a reporter during the G20 Innovation Ministerial on Sept. 2, 2026, in Chapel Hill, N.C. (Sean Rayford/Getty Images) · Sean Rayford via Getty Images The news, which had previously been reported but not yet confirmed by Nvidia itself, comes as the company increasingly looks to position itself as the so-called platform on which the rest of the AI tech stack operates. In comments on a call with analysts following the company's most recent earnings report, Huang described his view of Nvidia's positioning at the bedrock of the AI build-out as "one platform, fungible for every model and workload, durable for the entire life cycle of AI." "Nvidia's fully proven full-stack platform is uniquely suited to help sovereigns, neoclouds and enterprises build their AI infrastructure, bring it to full operation, continuously optimize it through CUDA software and connect it to offtake demand from our vast developer ecosystem," Huang said. "All of the AI services at some point are going to want to go around the world … I think they're going to run on NVIDIA all around the world." The acquisition of Hugging Face represents Nvidia's latest move to build and control the AI ecosystem, CFRA Research equity analyst Angelo Zino told Yahoo Finance. "I think it's less about the financials, at least today or even over the next 12, 18, 24 months, [and] it's more along the lines of building that AI ecosystem and trying to develop more and more capabilities and technology out there for the AI ecosystem, for physical AI, to really continue to come to fruition and build it out," Zino said. "Obviously, as the AI ecosystem grows, it ultimately translates to greater adoption, greater appetite and demand for what Nvidia is doing," Zino added. articles.title: Amazon.com vs. DraftKings: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026?
articles.content: Amazon.com vs. DraftKings: Which Consumer Stock Is a Better Buy in 2026? Pamela Kock, The Motley Fool Thu, September 3, 2026 at 10:29 AM EDT 6 min read DKNG AMZN Should you invest in a cloud and retail powerhouse or a fast-growing digital gaming leader? Choosing between Amazon.com (NASDAQ:AMZN) and DraftKings (NASDAQ:DKNG) depends on your preference for stability versus growth. Amazon dominates global e-commerce and cloud infrastructure while DraftKings captures a growing share of the legal U.S. sports betting market. These companies operate in different industries but compete for the same discretionary consumer dollars. This comparison examines their financial health and valuation to see which is a better fit for your portfolio. The case for Amazon.com Amazon focuses on e-commerce and cloud computing through its AWS division. The company serves a vast range of customers, from individual shoppers to government entities using its technology infrastructure. It relies on a network of third-party suppliers and shipping partners, particularly for components sourced from China, to maintain its dominance among retail stocks as it scales its logistics network. In its latest annual report, filed for FY 2025, revenue reached nearly $716.9 billion, representing a growth rate of approximately 12.4% over the prior year. The company reported a net income of close to $77.7 billion for the same period. This indicates a net margin of roughly 10.8%, which improved from the 9.3% net margin seen in 2024. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is roughly 1.1x, measuring the ability to pay short-term obligations with short-term assets. The debt-to-equity ratio, which compares total debt to shareholder equity, is approximately 0.4x. Amazon generated roughly $7.7 billion in free cash flow, representing cash remaining after capital expenditures are deducted from operating cash flow. The case for DraftKings DraftKings focuses on the digital entertainment and sports wagering market. It provides daily fantasy sports, online sportsbooks, and iGaming services to over 10 million users. To gain market access in various jurisdictions, the company maintains strategic relationships with local tribes and casinos. In FY 2025, revenue grew by nearly 27% to reach close to $6.1 billion. The company reported its first full year of profitability with a net income of approximately $3.7 million. This result represents a significant shift from the net loss of $507.3 million recorded in fiscal year 2024. As of its December 2025 balance sheet, the current ratio is roughly 1.0x. The debt-to-equity ratio is approximately 3.1x, suggesting the company uses a higher level of debt relative to its equity. Note that stock-based compensation represented roughly 51.2% of operating cash flow, which inflates reported cash generation since SBC is a non-cash expense added back in the cash flow statement. Story Continues Risk profile comparison Amazon faces intense competition across retail, advertising, and cloud computing. It also deals with significant regulatory scrutiny, including antitrust litigation from state officials and class action lawsuits regarding its marketplace practices. Operational risks include the complexity of its fulfillment network and its heavy reliance on third-party sellers and international suppliers. DraftKings operates in a highly competitive gaming industry against well-financed rivals. The company relies on third-party platforms like Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL) and cloud infrastructure from Amazon to reach its customers. It also manages risks from evolving state regulations, wagering excise tax audits, and its data feeds from providers such as Genius Sports (NYSE:GENI). Valuation comparison Amazon appears more conservatively valued on a future earnings basis, while DraftKings trades at a significant premium despite its lower price-to-sales multiple. The forward P/E ratio compares the stock price to future earnings estimates, providing a look at how much you pay for expected profits. The P/S ratio measures the stock price against total revenue, indicating how the market values every dollar of sales. Metric Amazon.com DraftKings Forward P/E 20.7x 189.3x P/S ratio 3.9x 2.1x Valuation metrics sourced from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers. Which stock would I buy in 2026? DraftKings is an undeniably interesting company, given the continued expansion of legal online sports betting and digital gaming in the United States. Its growth has been rapid, but investors should look closely at the quality of that growth. In 2025, DraftKings generated $662.9 million in operating cash flow; however, that figure included a $339.3 million add-back for stock-based compensation. Because stock-based compensation can dilute existing shareholders, the company's reported cash generation does not tell the whole story. DraftKings also ended the year with approximately $1.84 billion in long-term debt, although its substantial cash balance helps offset that obligation. Amazon is the less speculative choice. In 2025, it generated $716.9 billion in revenue and reported $77.7 billion in net income. Its scale, diversified revenue streams, and strong operating cash flow give it far more financial flexibility than DraftKings. The company is making a major investment in AI and cloud infrastructure, which has sharply reduced near-term free cash flow. That spending is not without risk, but it also supports the long-term competitiveness of AWS and Amazon's broader technology ecosystem. Given the choice between the two, I would buy Amazon. DraftKings offers greater upside if its expansion and profitability continue, but Amazon provides a more compelling combination of scale, financial resilience, diversified growth opportunities, and cash-generating strength. Of course, the better investment also depends on its valuation at the time of purchase. However, on business quality alone, Amazon is the clearer choice. articles.title: Whole Foods CEO bets on smaller stores and the latest Amazon tech to win over shoppers
articles.content: Whole Foods CEO bets on smaller stores and the latest Amazon tech to win over shoppers Brian Sozzi · Executive Editor Thu, September 3, 2026 at 10:06 AM EDT 6 min read AMZN WMT TGT KR Listen and subscribe to Power Players with Brian Sozzi on Apple Podcasts , Amazon Music , Spotify , YouTube , or wherever you find your favorite podcasts. Whole Foods received some rare praise on an Amazon ( AMZN ) earnings call dominated by talk about AI, Amazon Web Services, and some more AI. "If you look at the growth in geographies that Whole Foods Markets are in, they're significantly outpacing the growth of comparable grocers, and the profit trajectory continues to trend the right way as well," Amazon CEO Andy Jassy told analysts. "We found a new format there in Daily Shop in urban settings. It's off to an amazing start that we're expanding very rapidly." Indeed, the praise was well-deserved. The business appears to be doing well during a period in which competing grocers, such as Walmart ( WMT ), Target ( TGT ), and Kroger ( KR ), are locked in price wars and the US consumer continues to navigate food inflation. Second quarter sales in Amazon's physical stores segment — which is mostly Whole Foods' nearly 540 stores — grew 4% from the prior year. The company is aggressively opening up new locations, especially smaller sites in urban areas that offer more grab-and-go foods. It's also investing in technology to enhance the shopping experience. Whole Foods CEO Jason Buechel participates in a discussion at the Semafor World Economy 2026 summit on April 13, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images) · Kevin Dietsch via Getty Images At the helm of Whole Foods is CEO Jason Buechel. He joined the company in 2013 as chief information officer, where he spearheaded the grocery chain's digital infrastructure, e-commerce, and delivery capabilities before rising to COO. When Whole Foods co-founder John Mackey retired in September 2022, he handpicked Buechel as his successor. Buechel was recently promoted to vice president of Amazon Worldwide Grocery Stores, placing him in charge of unifying Whole Foods, Amazon Fresh, and Amazon Go under a cohesive retail strategy. "Having the opportunity to work side by side with John Mackey over those 11 months was also a great learning experience," Buechel said in a new episode of the Power Players With Brian Sozzi podcast (video above, listen below). "At the same time, a big thing that I did was something we called the Whole Conversations Tour, where I went out and visited with each one of our regions and connected with suppliers, customers, community members, all of our stakeholders to understand what are the most important things that we need to be focused on and what our greatest opportunities are as a company," Beuchel said. "And there are a couple areas we really wanted to double down on. One was reaccelerating growth. We'd been in kind of a space where we'd really pulled back on the number of new stores that we were opening," Story Continues Here are several notable excerpts from our chat with Buechel. On the new smaller-store Daily Shops concept: "As it relates to the Daily Shops, we've got 12 stores, six of them are in London, six here in the US — most in Manhattan. The store you shop at is about 40,000 to 45,000 square feet. We've got full-service offerings basically spread across the perimeter of meat, seafood, specialty cheese, prepared foods. And what we've done is taken the very best of Whole Foods and condense it down into what is closer to a 9,000-to-12,000-square-foot experience. By having a smaller footprint, we can be closer to where our customers are at. As you might imagine, especially in Manhattan, the ability to open a dozen more 40,000-square-foot stores is a very complicated process and would take years and years and hit probably a decade when we look at how complicated some of those projects can get. And the reality is, in this smaller footprint, we can move much quicker and help serve our customers' needs. And this is really allowing customers to quickly grab and go. A lot of this is really geared towards how our customers are shopping today, which is more frequently. They're not doing one large basket for a week or two. They're shopping on a regular basis. The average customer right now is shopping for food three to four times a week. And this new concept is really helping support that." On the potential for Daily Shops: "I see hundreds, quite frankly. This will be an opportunity where not only do we see this showing up in many dense urban areas across the country, but I think this concept will allow us to get to places that maybe we wouldn't be able to put a full-sized Whole Foods. I also think about things like college campuses." On the new Dash Carts: "Something that I'm excited about is some of the work that we've been doing right now with our Dash Carts. Earlier this year, we unveiled a brand-new version of our Amazon Dash Cart. It is 25% lighter than our previous version. It's got 40% more capacity. And it's really aimed to help serve sort of family-size shopping trips. And we've gotten tremendously positive feedback on customers because they can actually shop, check out, and bag their groceries all at once." On the "whole paycheck" moniker: "You're the first person to bring it up to me in a very long time at this point. And a lot of the folks who do, I sort of challenge them by saying 'Hey, I want you to … go to the store, do an honest comparison of like items, and tell me what you see.' I had a retail analyst who really challenged me about 18 months ago or so, and was trying to point out where he thought things were a lot better, and came back afterwards and was like, 'Hey, I might not have believed you exactly, but I was able to see it for myself.' And when you layer in the promotional side of it — and this is where the value really rings for customers — if you are a Prime member, you get that extra 10% off sale items." On high meat prices: "This is an area that we are focused on with suppliers. There's some macro challenges at play here that a lot of us aren't in control of. One of the things that we really lean into is making sure that we are absorbing as much of the costs we can ourselves before passing on to the customers. Hopefully you've noticed as you go to the meat case, we have some great value every single week in promotion." articles.title: Vulnerable Republicans urge Trump to unleash Maga Inc’s $400mn cash pile
articles.content: Donald Trump is sitting on a $400mn political war chest as fellow Republicans fight to keep power in Washington © Bloomberg Vulnerable Republicans urge Trump to unleash Maga Inc’s $400mn cash pile on x (opens in a new window) Vulnerable Republicans urge Trump to unleash Maga Inc’s $400mn cash pile on facebook (opens in a new window) Vulnerable Republicans urge Trump to unleash Maga Inc’s $400mn cash pile on linkedin (opens in a new window) Vulnerable Republicans urge Trump to unleash Maga Inc’s $400mn cash pile on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Vulnerable Republicans urge Trump to unleash Maga Inc’s $400mn cash pile on x (opens in a new window) Vulnerable Republicans urge Trump to unleash Maga Inc’s $400mn cash pile on facebook (opens in a new window) Vulnerable Republicans urge Trump to unleash Maga Inc’s $400mn cash pile on linkedin (opens in a new window) Vulnerable Republicans urge Trump to unleash Maga Inc’s $400mn cash pile on whatsapp (opens in a new window) Alex Rogers in Washington Published September 3 2026 Updated September 3 2026 Jump to comments section Print this page This is an on-site version of the White House Watch newsletter. You can read the previous edition here . Sign up for free here to get it on Tuesdays and Thursdays. Email us at [email protected] Good morning and welcome to White House Watch. In today’s newsletter: Struggling Republicans urge Trump to open $400mn war chest Pentagon chaos deepens after Dan Driscoll quits Justice department backs OpenAI in New York Times copyright battle Republicans in Congress are calling for Donald Trump’s $400mn political action committee, Maga Inc, to help save them . No president has had at his disposal a group with a greater war chest in a midterm election, when the party out of power typically dominates. But with only two months before election day , and Republican control of Congress on the line, the pro-Trump Super Pac has spent less than 1 per cent of its cash pile on political advertising since the start of 2025, and has not yet bought any significant future ad reservations, according to the latest Federal Election Commission filings and AdImpact data. “I think certainly any resources that are on our side of the political aisle should be deployed sooner rather than later,” Ryan Mackenzie, the Republican representing a crucial swing district in eastern Pennsylvania, including Bethlehem , told the FT. “If that’s what they were raising the funding for — to help our Republican team — they should make sure that it gets out as soon as possible.” Mike Collins, a Republican running for the US Senate in Georgia, acknowledged that Trump had rallied voters in his state but said money would be critical. Asked if he wanted Maga Inc’s help, Collins replied, “We’d love that, for sure.” “Trains run on coal,” Collins told the FT. “Campaigns run on gold.” Trump’s political adviser James Blair has indicated that the money would go to cash-hungry Republicans. Blair texted the FT: “They’re in luck!” Programming note: White House Watch will be taking a break for the US Labor Day holiday. We’ll be back in your inbox on Thursday September 10. The latest headlines Federal Reserve governor Chris Waller has said he would be “inclined” to keep interest rates on hold , highlighting divisions among the US central bank’s governors as they prepare for a crucial vote this month. Chevron has committed to more than double its oil production in Venezuela over the next five years in a $7bn plan , in the first big investment from a US major in the Latin American country since the Trump administration toppled former leader Nicolás Maduro. The Trump administration has made an extraordinary intervention in a legal battle between The New York Times and OpenAI, siding with the $852bn AI group to reject the newspaper’s claims of copyright infringement. A federal judge ruled that Google will not have to divest crucial parts of its digital advertising arm, rejecting the Department of Justice’s argument that a forced sale is the only way to dismantle its monopoly over the business. The rapid adoption of AI has led to “unusually high levels” of unemployment among college graduates in Texas, the US state with the most data centre capacity under construction, according to research. Gloria Steinem, the pioneering feminist activist, has died aged 92 . What we’re hearing US Army secretary Dan Driscoll’s last day was on Wednesday. He handed his resignation to Trump earlier in the week with a blunt message about Pete Hegseth’s interference in the largest branch of America’s military, report my colleagues Steff Chávez and James Politi. Driscoll, a close friend of vice-president JD Vance, believed Hegseth was causing “generational damage” to the army, according to a person familiar with his thinking. He “had tried so many different ways and so many different times, but it was just clear that . . . Hegseth wasn’t willing to listen to the facts or the truth, or the reason, or any of that, because of his personal animosity”, the person said. The departure of the army’s top civilian official was the culmination of months of tension with the defence secretary about the force’s technological transformation and senior military appointments, as well as intractable personal tensions between the two men. Hegseth has purged two dozen generals and admirals since the start of Trump’s second term through firings or forced removals. Thom Tillis, the retiring North Carolina Republican senator, sharply criticised Hegseth in a post on X. “He is creating a leadership void at the top of our military ranks,” posted Tillis. “I have never witnessed more inept management of the brave men and women who serve our country.” “He is intimidated by competence and retreats to ginning up culture wars instead of soberly attending to the vital work of our national defence and the health and wellbeing of our fighting force.” Sean Parnell, the Pentagon spokesperson, told the FT that “the premise that the department is in disarray is completely baseless and an insult to every dedicated professional and warfighter in this building who comes to work every day to defend this nation”. Parnell added that “this is what reform looks like” and “the department operates on a disciplined ‘next man up’ mentality and is firing on all cylinders under secretary Hegseth’s leadership”. Viewpoints Martin Wolf argues the wheels are coming off the US world order. Stephen Foley reports on the “extraordinary outpouring of opposition” to the Securities and Exchange Commission’s plan to scrap quarterly reporting . The FT editorial board writes that Trump’s oil deal with Venezuela is the wrong way to revive the South American nation’s economy. articles.content: Standard Chartered Launches Spot Bitcoin, Ether Trading for UAE Institutions Editorial Staff Thu, September 3, 2026 at 1:43 PM EDT 2 min read STAN.L BTC-USD ETH-USD ETH BTC Standard Chartered ($STAN) has launched spot trading in Bitcoin (CRYPTO: $BTC) and Ether (CRYPTO: $ETH) for institutional clients in the United Arab Emirates, making it the first global systemically important bank (G-SIB) to offer the service in the country. In a Thursday announcement , the bank said that eligible institutional clients can trade BTC and ETH through its electronic trading channels integrated into the bank's existing platforms, allowing clients to access crypto trading through the same foreign exchange interfaces they already use. Unlike futures or other derivatives, spot trading involves buying and selling the underlying asset for delivery. articles.title: A new wave of VC funds bets on female founders
articles.content: A new wave of VC funds bets on female founders Invest in women taskforce.webp Leah Hodgson Thu, September 3, 2026 at 1:35 PM EDT 2 min read Featured image courtesy of the Invest in Women Taskforce Female-focused VC funds are piling up this year as women-founded startups pull in more capital. On Sep. 1, Berlin-based investor Auxxo closed its second Female Catalyst Fund at €33.3 million (around $38.7 million) to back pre-seed and seed female-founded startups. The vehicle, which is one of the largest direct funds dedicated to female founders in Europe, follows several fund launches and closes in the space this year. In May, Arāya Sie Fund, a joint venture between London-based VC Arāya Ventures and accelerator Sie Ventures , secured £7.5 million (around $10 million) in its first close. Around a month earlier, the Women Backing Women fund, a fund-of-funds managed by Bootstrap4F and created by the UK's Invest in Women Taskforce, raised £130 million in its first close. In April, Copenhagen-based Unconventional Ventures announced the second close of its Fund II, which targets diverse founders, including women. This new wave of female-focused vehicles comes amid a funding surge. Deal value currently stands at €9.7 billion this year, according to PitchBook's European VC female founders dashboard , almost reaching 2025's annual total. At the current pace, 2026 is tracking to be the third-highest year for female founders in terms of capital. Mirroring the wider European market, deal count is set to fall short of 2025's figure. Funding for female founders is increasingly leaning into deep-tech areas, such as semiconductors, robotics and quantum. In June, French quantum computing startup Quobly raised a €115 million Series A, while Barcelona-based AI robotics company Theker secured an $85 million Series A. AI is another standout area. London-based AI video startup Synthesia raised its $200 million Series E in January at a $4 billion valuation. UK-based AI infrastructure company Volta announced in August that it had raised $300 million via a seed round and a Series A, valuing the company at $2.4 billion. While more capital is heading into female-founded startups, their share of overall investment remains small. All-female founding teams accounted for just 1% of deal value this year, down from 1.3% in 2025. Mixed teams have seen a modest bump to 16.3% from 15% in 2025, but are still below previous years' levels. articles.title: Bitcoin tops $80,000: 'Crypto winter is close to being over'
articles.content: Bitcoin tops $80,000: 'Crypto winter is close to being over' Ines Ferré · Senior Business Reporter Thu, September 3, 2026 at 1:32 PM EDT 2 min read BTC-USD Investors got a hopeful signal on Thursday that bitcoin ( BTC-USD ) may defy its historically weak September trend. The world's largest cryptocurrency jumped 4% on Thursday to rise above $80,000 as worries about a Federal Reserve rate hike eased and Treasury yields dropped. The question is whether the token can remain above these levels, given that bitcoin has historically posted negative returns in September in nine of the past 15 years. More from Yahoo Scout How has bitcoin performed during September historically? What are analysts' price targets for bitcoin? What factors could drive bitcoin's price movement? Why did bitcoin surge above $80,000 on Thursday? "It's important data, and we should respect it," Fundstrat head of digital assets Sean Farrell said. However, the strategist noted that the token has "bucked" this historical monthly trend over the past few years. "We haven't seen a negative September in four years, and seasonality — it's a helpful data point, but it is not a foolproof system for trading these markets," he said. Bitcoin surged on Thursday. The token is coming off a strong August rally, prompting some strategists to suggest that the crypto bear market may have bottomed out or is nearing one. "The recent BTC price movement suggests that the crypto winter is close to being over," Noelle Acheson, author of "Crypto Is Macro Now," told Yahoo Finance. The token rallied 25% last month as the Treasury Department's recent intervention in the bond market and assistance to Japan helped lift the prices of gold and crypto assets. Some of those gains were given back as oil prices surged and hawkish comments from Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh raised concerns about the Fed's upcoming September rate decision. On Thursday, Fed governor Christopher Waller hinted he would support keeping rates unchanged if inflation eases. "I could see crypto and broader equities mounting a rally post-FOMC that could take bitcoin to a higher level than today into late September, early October, " David Grider, head of liquid investments at Finality Capital, told Yahoo Finance. Grider said the move would be driven by either a surprise Fed rate hold or by yields falling sharply after the first rate hike. The risk of a market correction still holds, in which case bitcoin would also be sold off. But crypto analysts see such a move as short-term. "So long as the Treasury is willing to intervene in the yield curve, we believe, the bid on 'hard assets' such as bitcoin stays," Bernstein analyst Gautam Chhugani wrote in a recent note. Chhugani and his team called a bottom for bitcoin earlier this year and have placed a $150,000 year-end price target on the token. With the exception of 2018 and last year, the fourth quarter has proven bullish for bitcoin.
